::: {.panel-tabset .nav-pills} ## Intro Differential calculus is a subject in mathematics that aims to understand mathematical functions by studying their "derivatives". There are many interpretations of the derivative, and the study of calculus finds numerous applications in the physical sciences, engineering, and of course data science and machine learning (among other fields). #### What is a mathematical function? The word "function" has many uses in colloquial English. In day-to-day use, it might mean the purpose or individual role of an object; in computer science, it refers to a reusable block of code that performs a specific action. The word "function" when used in math class might bring to mind sines, cosines, logarithms or polynomials. We might also think of graphs of functions, x and y axes, and various formulas we have learned to write down. But how exactly do we define a mathematical function? It turns out that the formal definition is very broad-- a mathematical function is just a box that takes some possible inputs, and for each input it spits out an output. Any black box will do, as long as giving the same input many times will always result in the same output (in other words, no "randomness"). For example, we could have a function that takes in English words as input and returns their first letter as output ("apple" --> "a"), or a function that takes a location on the surface of the Earth as input and returns as output the mean surface temperature at that location on May 15, 1985.

::: {#fig-func-def} ![](../../static/module1/func-def.png){width="50%"} A black box :::


Formulas like sin(x), ex and x2+1 are recipes for constructing functions. They tell you what happens inside the black box. For example, if I write f(x) = x2+1, that defines a function that takes real numbers as input, and for any input returns the "square plus one" (another real number) as output. Some functions have nice recipes (like x2+1), while others (like surface temperature on Earth) may not have any such recipe, and we may not know how to calculate them! An ML engineer working on autonomous driving might be interested in the function that takes an image of a road as input and outputs whether or not a person is visible standing in the middle of it. This function probably also doesn't have an exact formula, so the engineer will try to approximate it with whatever ingredients they can find. #### Inputs, Outputs and Sensitivity As we mentioned before, there are many ways to interpret the derivative (for some examples, see pages 3 and 4 of this writeup). Each interpretation gives different insight, even if they are all formally equivalent in the end. Most commonly, the derivative of a function at a point is described as the "instantaneous rate of change" of the function at that point. Stated another way, it measures the "sensitivity" of the function to its input. If I wiggle the input knob on my black box, how rapidly does the output needle swing? If the derivative is large, my function is like a bike in high gear-- even a slight push on the pedals (input) gives a large rotation of the wheel (output).

::: {#fig-smallder} ![](../../static/module1/smallder.png){width="50%"} A function with a small positive derivative. :::


A constant derivative equal to 2 means any change in input would always give twice the size of change in the output, while a derivative like 0.00001 suggests that increasing the input would only increase the output a little. A negative derivative means increasing the input will decrease the output, at least in the neighbourhood of the point we are interested in.

::: {#fig-negder} ![](../../static/module1/negder.png){width="50%"} A function with a large and negative derivative :::


Since the "sensitivity" of a function can change over its various possible inputs, we generally talk about the derivative of a function at a point. When we say "the derivative of sine is cosine", we mean that if our original function is given by the recipe "f(x) = sin(x)", then there is also a nice recipe that tells us the derivative at each possible input, namely the recipe "f'(x) = cos(x)". So if we want to know the inputs where sin(x) is increasing, we can look for the points where cos(x) is positive. #### Your next task Use the tabs at the top of this page to view the two supplemental videos--- they will guide you through developing some of this intuition for derivatives. Once you are ready, click the button on the bottom right below to test your understanding with some short exercises. ## Video 1 ## Video 2 :::
